title: Pricing by hours per project for Window cleaning (all heights)
audience: Owners and crew leads who quote window cleaning jobs and need a price that covers cost, travel, access and a margin.
learningOutcomes: Calculate a cost per productive hour for a window round from your own figures
Estimate window job hours by storey and access, including set-up, travel and checking time
Build a quote from hours, a rate and a margin, and state its basis, storey lines and exclusions

instruction.heading: Why hours are the starting unit for windows
instruction.body: A window round is mostly time: travel between sites, set-up of ladders or poles, the clean itself, and a check in daylight. Storey and access change the time more than the number of panes does. Hours make that visible. Start from hours, and check the result against the lead-generation estimates only afterwards.

instruction.heading: Build your cost per productive hour
instruction.body: Divide the total cost of running the round over a period by the chargeable hours in that period. Include wages with on-costs, the vehicle, ladders and pole kit, water and cleaning consumables, insurance, phone, software and administration. Use chargeable hours only. Employee pay rates and on-costs may be set by an award or enterprise agreement; that point is unconfirmed in this research, so check it for each worker before you use any figure.

instruction.heading: Estimate the hours by task
instruction.body: Split each job into tasks: exterior panes by storey, interior panes, tracks and screens, set-up for each storey, travel between sites, and a checking allowance. Estimate each in a range. Add a set allowance for delays such as a blocked gate or a client who is not home. Xero's guide suggests 10 to 20 per cent for unexpected work (stated by the source, and the BP-05 research flags whether that range is acceptable). Record actual hours after each job, with the reason for any difference.

instruction.heading: Turn hours into a price
instruction.body: Multiply the total hours by the cost per productive hour to get the job cost. Divide the cost by one minus your target margin to get the price, so a 25 per cent margin on price means dividing by 0.75. Apply your minimum charge and materials policy. Show storey and access as named lines, not as a hidden surcharge. Marketplace percentages for access (20 to 40 per cent) and storeys (15 to 30 per cent) are unmeasured claims, so use your own hours for those lines.

instruction.heading: Check the price against the market, without copying it
instruction.body: The lead-generation guide gives a Melbourne hourly band for standard residential window work of $42 to $84, averaging $58, and $84 to $210 for high-rise or rope access, typically $135 (What's The Damage, verified November 2026). It is an estimate, not a cost, and it says nothing about your access method. Use it to ask whether your hours are realistic, not to set your rate.

instruction.heading: Keep the quote honest
instruction.body: A window quote states the scope by storey, the hours or price basis, the exclusions, what the client must provide (access, water, clear sills), and how long the quote is valid. Do not show the internal cost per hour unless your policy says to. Re-quote when the scope changes. A quote without exclusions, especially for storeys, leads to disputes.

procedure: Gather the year's total round costs and the chargeable hours achieved in the same period.
Divide total costs by chargeable hours to get the cost per productive hour.
Break the job into exterior and interior panes by storey, tracks, set-up, travel and checking, and estimate each as a range.
Add a set delay allowance, sized from your own records.
Multiply total hours by the cost per productive hour, then divide by one minus the margin.
Apply the materials policy and the minimum charge.
Write the quote with scope by storey, hours basis, exclusions, client inputs and validity.
Record actual hours after each job and compare them with the estimate.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative figures only, not market rates. A two-storey home with 15 windows, cleaned inside and out. The owner estimates 2.5 hours on site, 0.5 hours of travel and 0.5 hours of set-up and checking, a total of 3.5 hours. The owner's cost per productive hour is $60 AUD (illustrative). The target margin on price is 25 per cent (illustrative).
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the job cost, what is the price with a 25 per cent margin on price, and what changes if a blocked gate adds 2 hours?
workedExamples.reasoning: The cost is 3.5 hours multiplied by $60 AUD, which is $210 AUD. The price is $210 divided by 0.75, which is $280 AUD. At the lead-generation Melbourne average of $58 an hour, $280 AUD equals about 4.8 hours of bare labour, so the gap is the travel, set-up and checking time that the hourly band does not show. A blocked gate adds 2 hours, which raises the cost to $330 AUD and the price to $440 AUD, but only if the quote's access terms allow that time to be charged. Check those terms before adding it to the bill.

equipmentAndPpe: Quote worksheet or spreadsheet with a line for each storey
Time log for each job, with estimated and actual columns
Measuring tape or laser measure for pane counts
PPE and access equipment as listed in {{business:safety.required_ppe}}, and the working-at-height method for each storey

commonErrors.error: Pricing from the hourly wage alone
commonErrors.prevention: Include on-costs, vehicle, ladder and pole kit, consumables, insurance and administration in the cost per productive hour.

commonErrors.error: Counting paid hours as productive hours
commonErrors.prevention: Use chargeable hours only when calculating the cost per productive hour.

commonErrors.error: Copying a marketplace access or storey percentage instead of timing the access
commonErrors.prevention: Time each storey from your own jobs and show the line with its reason.

commonErrors.error: Quoting with no exclusions for storeys, access or water supply
commonErrors.prevention: List what is excluded, what the client provides and the access assumptions.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Pricing guidance only. The ACCC says misleading price statements are prohibited. State and territory fair trading rules also apply.

Victoria: the working-at-height rule for storeys was not checked in this draft. Before you allow time for a storey, check the Victorian rule with WorkSafe Victoria. The Commonwealth code (2015) and the NSW code (2019) are cited elsewhere and are not Victorian rules.
Award, enterprise agreement and on-cost rates for employees are unconfirmed in this research. Check which instrument applies to each worker before using any cost figure.

qualityStandard: Each quote shows scope by storey, hours or price basis, exclusions, client inputs and validity.
The cost per productive hour is calculated from the owner's own records and dated.
Actual hours are recorded for at least the first ten window jobs of each storey band and compared with the estimate.
documentationEvidence: Cost per productive hour worksheet, dated, with the source of each figure
Quote showing storey scope, hours basis, exclusions and validity
Job time log with estimated and actual hours by storey
summary: A window round is mostly time, so start every quote from hours.
Cost per productive hour uses chargeable time, not paid time.
Storey, access, travel and checking time are named lines, not hidden extras.
Compare estimates with actual hours, and change the method when they diverge.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which costs belong in the cost per productive hour for a window round?
options: Only the hourly wage of the lowest-paid worker and nothing else from the accounts or the rent
The price the client pays, plus the deposit, the late fee and the crew bonus paid
The average hourly rate of competitors in the local area and their fees for the whole year
Wages with on-costs, vehicle, ladder and pole kit, consumables, insurance and administration, divided by chargeable hours

knowledgeChecks.question: A two-storey job is estimated at 3.5 hours and takes 5. What is the right response?
options: Record the actual hours, find the cause, and adjust the estimate and future quotes
Leave the estimate, since the client has already paid and the crew has finished
Reduce paid hours for the crew on the next job and skip the morning break
Raise the price for this client's next job only and no one else is charged more

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does a window quote need an exclusions list?
options: To hide the margin from the client and to keep the rates a secret from the crew
To make the quote longer and to fill up the page with more text and words for the client
To show what the price covers, so scope changes can be priced and disputes are reduced
To lower the client's expectations and to make the job seem much smaller than it is

sourceReferences: What's The Damage, 'Window cleaning cost Melbourne', https://whatsthedamage.com.au/window-cleaning-cost-melbourne/, verified November 2026, metadata 2026-11-01. Lead-generation guide; hourly bands are estimates. Used for the hourly band only.

business.gov.au, 'Choose a pricing strategy', https://business.gov.au/products-and-services/choose-a-pricing-strategy, page metadata dated 1 October 2026. Supports: on-costs such as leave and superannuation belong in the hourly cost.
ACCC, 'Setting prices: what's allowed', https://www.accc.gov.au/business/pricing/setting-prices-whats-allowed, last modified 15 July 2026. Supports: misleading price statements are prohibited.

Xero Australia, 'How to price services', https://www.xero.com/au/guides/how-to-price-services/, dated 3 September 2026. Supports: divide by billable hours, not total hours; add a set allowance for delays; figure stated by source of 10 to 20 per cent for unexpected work.

Carters Trade Leader, 'Estimating how many hours a job will take', https://tradeleader.carters.co.nz/trade-skills/estimating-how-many-hours-a-job-will-take-why-83-get-it-wrong/, dated 1 October 2025. New Zealand publisher; general method only.

Work Health and Safety (Managing the Risk of Falls at Workplaces) Code of Practice 2015, https://legislation.gov.au/F2016L00425/asmade/2016-03-30/text/original/epub/OEBPS/document_1/document_1.html, registered 2016. Commonwealth code; not Victorian law. Cited for the height point; the Victorian rule was not checked.

WorkSafe Victoria, news release on falls risks in the solar sector, https://www.worksafe.vic.gov.au/news/2026-08/crackdown-falls-risks-solar-sector, 26 August 2026. Supports: allowing workers onto a roof without adequate protection is unlawful, even with no incident. Aimed at solar; the principle is stated for any roof.

Note: award, enterprise agreement, on-cost and state fair trading rules for window work are UNCONFIRMED. Victorian working-at-height rules were not checked. No window-specific hours benchmark was found.
